method: Reuses the research from emp_overtime.json (checked 2026-08-20), not a fresh search -- the two clauses make close to the same claim about the same federal rule, and re-reading the same two opinions to answer the same question would be busywork rather than diligence. What is new here is reading ea_overtime's own body against that same case law, since the flagged gap in emp_overtime was explicitly that this clause deserved its own pass rather than being assumed covered. Egress to 29 U.S.C. section 207 itself remained blocked at check time (re-probed the same day, unchanged).
queries: (reused) Forrester v. Roth's I.G.A. Foodliner overtime (CourtListener, 9th Cir.), opinion 389336
(reused) Chao v. Gotham Registry, Inc. (CourtListener, 2d Cir.), opinion 9613742

assertions.text: the role is non-exempt and overtime is owed as required by federal law and the law of the operating state
assertions.note: Correct as a matter of the FLSA's coverage structure, but the clause does not itself state the 1.5x-over-40 rule the way emp_overtime does -- it defers entirely to 'as required by federal law and the law of {{opStateLong}}'. Nothing to contradict or corroborate beyond confirming the deferral names a real rule rather than an empty one; see emp_overtime's assertion on the same point for the rule itself.

assertions.text: overtime actually worked will be paid whether or not it was approved in advance
assertions.note: Same claim as emp_overtime, same gap. Forrester, 646 F.2d at 414 (9th Cir. 1981): the duty to pay attaches only once the employer 'knows or should have known' the work happened; Chao, 514 F.3d at 287 (2d Cir. 2008), to the same effect. Both cases also confirm the flip side this clause omits: an employee who conceals the hours or bypasses the approval/reporting channel entirely, preventing the employer from finding out, may leave the employer owing nothing -- the exact fact pattern Forrester affirmed summary judgment on.

assertions.text: requiring advance approval for overtime is itself lawful, so long as approved-or-not the hours worked are still paid
assertions.note: Chao, 514 F.3d at 288-291, discussing Reich v. Department of Conservation and Natural Resources (11th Cir.): an employer 'could not avoid overtime compensation simply by adopting a policy against overtime and issuing periodic warnings' -- the policy itself is fine, only using it as a reason not to pay is not. This is exactly the distinction the clause's own rationale draws ('discipline for working it is permissible; refusing to pay for it is not') and it holds up.

gaps: Same omission as emp_overtime, worth restating in this clause's own terms because the audience is different: this is language in an offer letter, read by a new hire before they have worked a single shift, not an internal handbook policy read by someone already employed. Telling a new hire overtime 'will be paid whether or not it was approved' with no qualifier is the more consequential place for the gap to sit, since it sets an expectation the company may not always be able to meet -- specifically where the new hire never reports the hours through whatever channel the company actually uses.
29 U.S.C. section 207 and section 203(g) were not independently fetched -- every host that would carry them was blocked, same as for emp_overtime.
The clause's deferral to 'the law of {{opStateLong}}' was not checked against any state's actual daily-overtime or other overtime rules -- it names no specific state rule to verify.

judicialQuotations.case: Forrester v. Roth's I.G.A. Foodliner, Inc. (9th Cir. 1981) 646 F.2d 413
judicialQuotations.quote: an employer who knows or should have known that an employee is or was working overtime must comply with the provisions of section 207. An employer who is armed with this knowledge cannot stand idly by and allow an employee to perform overtime work without proper compensation, even if the employee does not make a claim for the overtime compensation.

judicialQuotations.case: Chao v. Gotham Registry, Inc. (2d Cir. 2008) 514 F.3d 280
judicialQuotations.quote: It is clear an employer's actual or imputed knowledge that an employee is working is a necessary condition to finding the employer suffers or permits that work.
